2c-x.note: All three quotes are on the pages as given. FRANK: 'The 2C family of drugs are classed as psychedelics (hallucinogens) but they can also produce stimulant effects'; ADF, same section as anchor 2: 'The '2C' group of drugs are psychedelics but can also cause stimulant effects'. The line is close to that ADF sentence in build but shares no run longer than three words with either page, so I leave it. Someone who has only heard the name learns it is a group of psychedelics with stimulant effects; the line does not say where the drugs come from, and no checked passage says it (ADF only calls the group 'a general name for phenethylamines').

2c-x.line: People can feel alert and warm towards others, and notice colours, sounds and smells more than usual.
2c-x.note: Anchors confirmed and the content is supported, but the line is FRANK's wording joined together: 'feel awake, alert and affectionate' (five words in a row from its sentence) and 'aware of colours, sounds and smells' (six words in a row from its bullet). The corrected line says the same and no more in our own words; hedge kept ('can').

FRANK: 'normally sold as pills or powders, but this can vary'; ADF: '2C-B usually comes as a white powder or crystal and is sometimes pressed into a tablet similar to MDMA'. Nexus is in both lists of other names. Longest shared run is five words ('a white powder or crystal'), a plain list of forms.

benzodiazepines.line: Benzodiazepines, or benzos, are depressants: drugs that make the brain and body work more slowly.
benzodiazepines.note: All three anchors confirmed. The line repeats ADF's stock family sentence: twelve words in a row ('they slow down the messages travelling between the brain and the body'). The corrected line says what 'depressant' means in our own words, as FRANK ('slow the brain and body down') and EUDA ('depressants of the central nervous system') support it. The first line does tell a newcomer what the drug is.

ADF sentence in full: prescribed by doctors 'for short-term or intermittent use to relieve the symptoms of certain health conditions, including anxiety or panic disorders, insomnia, alcohol withdrawal, and epilepsy'. 'Lab-made' rests on EUDA's 'synthetic substances'. NIDA entry 'Benzodiazepines' on the A to Z page confirmed. Own words; longest shared run four words (a list of conditions).

All four confirmed (ADF list stands under the sub-heading 'Effects', after the words 'Effects can include:'). The line is near ADF's 'Depressants can make people feel calm, relaxed and drowsy', but it is three plain effect words that FRANK ('Sleepy, relaxed, calm') and EUDA ('calm ... drowsiness and sleep') also give; longest shared run four words. Left as ok; the editor may reorder the three words if wanted.

ADF: 'Benzos most commonly come as a round or oval shaped pill'; 'known by their chemical (generic) name (e.g. Diazepam) or their brand name (e.g. Valium®)'. FRANK and EUDA give tablets, capsules and injections. Own words.

cannabis.note: All six quotes found where stated (EUDA heading 'About cannabis', profile dated 08.05.2013; NIDA entry headed 'Cannabis'). The line says no more than they say and is in our own words. One word is not plain: 'psychoactive'. The same pages allow a plainer wording if the editor wants one (ADF, next sentence after anchor 1: 'It's the component in cannabis that makes you feel 'high''; NIDA: 'intoxicating—mind altering—effects'), for example 'the chemical behind most of its high is THC'. The first line says where cannabis comes from and what is in it; with line 1 a newcomer understands what it is.

ADF list under 'Effects of cannabis (THC)' > 'Effects', after 'Effects can include:' has 'relaxation and euphoria', 'laughter and excitement', 'increased appetite', 'feeling tired or drowsy'. FRANK 'How you might feel': 'Stoned', happy, giggly and/or sleepy, confused, paranoid. Each of the five words in the line is supported; own words; hedged.

All six confirmed. ADF's list is introduced by 'The THC extracted from a cannabis plant can come in many different forms, including:'. FRANK sub-headings are 'Weed' and 'Hash/hashish'. EUDA 'Other names': herbal cannabis and resin 'formally known as marijuana and hashish (or just 'hash')'. Forms and names only; own words.

ADF sentence in full: 'Medical cannabis is prescribed to relieve the symptoms of chronic or cancer-related pain, multiple sclerosis (MS), epilepsy, Tourette syndrome, and a range of other health conditions.' The line is a shortened form of it (longest shared run four words: 'Medical cannabis is prescribed'), not its wording. Epilepsy rests on ADF alone. The EUDA sentence (2013 profile) is about herbal cannabis sold on prescription in the Netherlands; the FRANK sentence stands under 'The law' but the line states no law.

dxm.note: All three confirmed (NIDA page shows 'December 2017'; MedlinePlus 'Last Revised - 01/15/2022'). ADF and NIDA give almost the same sentence ('is a cough suppressant found in many over the counter cold medications' / '... OTC cold medicines'); the line keeps its build but puts each term in plain words (cough medicine, cold remedies, sold without a prescription), longest shared run four words, so I leave it. A newcomer understands what DXM is. The lines never use the family word: ADF says 'When taken in high doses, DXM acts as a dissociative' and lists DXM under 'Examples of dissociatives'; left out, rightly, because that sentence is tied to an amount.

dxm.line: As a medicine, it eases a cough by making the brain area that triggers coughing less active.
dxm.note: Both anchors confirmed and the content is right, but the line copies ten words in a row from MedlinePlus ('activity in the part of the brain that causes coughing'), a page whose medicine texts are licensed from a publisher. The corrected line says the same and no more in our own words.

ADF list under 'Effects of DXM' is introduced by 'Effects start within 30-60 minutes and last for around six hours, and may include:' and has the bullets 'euphoria' and 'increase in positive mood'; the page says it 'looks at the non-medical use of DXM'. NIDA sub-heading 'DXM': 'Short-term effects of DXM misuse can range from mild stimulation to alcohol- or marijuana-like intoxication'. Hedge kept ('may'); no amount; own words.

ADF: 'It can also come in the form of cough syrup, gel capsules, lozenges, soft pastilles and pills'; other names 'DM, Robo, Robotripping, skittling, dex.' ADF Dissociatives page, heading 'Examples of dissociatives': 'It is sold in syrup, tablet, spray, and lozenge forms.' MedlinePlus sentence confirmed. Forms and names only.

ghb-gbl.note: All five confirmed (FRANK page heading 'GHB & GBL'; NIDA entry 'GHB'). Own words, longest shared run five words ('into GHB in the body', FRANK); the stock ADF sentence about messages is rightly not used. For a newcomer the first line works only if the word 'depressant' is already known: it is not explained in this drug's lines (line 1 gives 'relaxed, drowsy'). The sources would support a few plain words for it (FRANK: 'similar sedative and anaesthetic effects'; ADF: 'Depressants can make a person feel calm, relaxed and drowsy'), if the editor finds room within 20 words.

ADF list (sub-heading 'Effects', after 'Effects can include:'): 'increased happiness and confidence', 'relaxation', 'drowsiness'. FRANK list after 'GHB and GBL can make you feel:': euphoric, drowsy, relaxed, turned on/sexy. All four words of the line are supported; own words; hedged.

ADF: 'GHB usually comes as a colourless, odourless, bitter or salty liquid, often sold in small bottles or vials'; other names begin 'G, fantasy, grievous bodily harm (GBH), juice, liquid ecstasy'. FRANK: sold as 'colourless oily liquids'; also called '1, 4-Bd, Gbh, Gbl, Geebs, Liquid Ecstasy'. Longest shared run five words ('usually comes as a colourless'), a plain statement of form.

FRANK (under 'What does it look like?'): 'GHB has a medical use in the treatment of narcolepsy'. NIDA: 'a depressant approved for use in the treatment of narcolepsy, a disorder that causes daytime "sleep attacks"'. Own words. 'Narcolepsy' is left unexplained; NIDA's words would support adding 'a sleep disorder'.
